Hello all, 

I am running a simple model to test linear growth across for time points, with random slopes and intercepts (see below). I believe I have done everything correctly, but i get the lavaan warning that the covariance matrix of latent variables in not positive definite. Nicolas--
When you create the slope as a factor, you turn a model parameter into a variable. Then this variable must have a variance, which is differences in the value of the slope across respondents. A fixed coefficient slope model is one where there is no variation in slope across respondents. But if there is 0 variance in the slope coefficient, then it can't be used to predict dependent variables. So you might try simply deleting the slope factor from your model.

I admit, I don't know how to use lavaan to specify a model with random intercept and nonrandom, nonzero slope. Sorry.
--Ed Rigdon

messages.subject: Re: Confusion about lavaan warning: covaraince of latent variables not positive definte
parts:
Nicolas,
I am not sure that you question has a matter of fact answer because it is a matter of accepted practice which may vary by literature.  Here are some thoughts.

One thing that you could do is to extract the sample means, implied means, and mean residuals.  Plotting the first two against time might make a convincing case, particularly combined with the fact that the linear model does not reach a valid solution.

One thing that I notice is that your variable names begin with 'sqr'.  If that stands for square root (or square) you might consider analyzing the variables without the transformation to see if the non-linearity goes away.

You are somewhat limited by having only four time points.  In future studies, if you can collect more time points, you might consider adding a second slope that has fixed zero loadings up until the time point represented by your 3rd time point and then has a linear slope (piecewise growth) or adding a second slope affecting all time points with loadings equal to the square of the linear loadings (quadratic polynomial growth).  Free loadings are not really testing a specific nonlinear hypothesis but just an unspecific alternative hypothesis to the linear null.

You could try constraining the variances to be non-negative and refitting the linear growth model.  I think that it is fair to say that majority opinion has come down on the side that this is not good general practice because it tends to hide problems with the model.  However, in your situation, it may be a useful follow-up to fitting the model without the non-negativitiy constraints.  It might not converge at all but it if does it may give you a poorly fitting solution that passes basic admissibility tests.

I am not a statistician but it seems to me that the following logic holds.  The inadmissible solution represents the best obtainable fit (assuming you get a consistent solution) for the unconstrained linear growth model.  As such, any admissible solution would have to fit worse.  So, if the nonlinear growth model fits better at a statistically significant level, then it must also fit better than any admissible solution for the linear growth model.  However, it may be helpful to compare the inadmissible solution to an admissible solution with constraints, because you would not accept the inadmissible solution even if it fit well, or within sampling error of the non-linear growth model.  Perhaps others can comment on the behavior of chi-square for inadmissible solutions and the validity of such chi-square difference tests.

Keith

Keith A. Markus
John Jay College of Criminal Justice, CUNY
http://jjcweb.jjay.cuny.edu/kmarkus
Frontiers of Test Validity Theory: Measurement, Causation and Meaning.
http://www.routledge.com/books/details/9781841692203/

parts:
Oh the basic solution was that the model was mis-specified. 

Originally, i forced the slope into a linear trend (i.e. s.PH =~ 0*sqrev_phT1 + 1*sqrev_phT2 + 3*sqrev_phT3 + 4*sqrev_phT4).

I then tried to let it freely estimate (i.e. s.PH =~ 0*sqrev_phT1 + 1*sqrev_phT2 + ?*sqrev_phT3 + ?*sqrev_phT4) which suggested a non-linear trend (specifically --  s.PH =~ 0*sqrev_phT1 + 1*sqrev_phT2 + .5*sqrev_phT3 + .5*sqrev_phT4). Once i used either the free estimation or the non-linear trend it solved the issue.

On Tue, Apr 3, 2018 at 6:42 AM kmarkus via lavaan <lav...@googlegroups.com> wrote:
Nicolas,
I am not sure that you question has a matter of fact answer because it is a matter of accepted practice which may vary by literature.  Here are some thoughts.

One thing that you could do is to extract the sample means, implied means, and mean residuals.  Plotting the first two against time might make a convincing case, particularly combined with the fact that the linear model does not reach a valid solution.

One thing that I notice is that your variable names begin with 'sqr'.  If that stands for square root (or square) you might consider analyzing the variables without the transformation to see if the non-linearity goes away.

You are somewhat limited by having only four time points.  In future studies, if you can collect more time points, you might consider adding a second slope that has fixed zero loadings up until the time point represented by your 3rd time point and then has a linear slope (piecewise growth) or adding a second slope affecting all time points with loadings equal to the square of the linear loadings (quadratic polynomial growth).  Free loadings are not really testing a specific nonlinear hypothesis but just an unspecific alternative hypothesis to the linear null.

You could try constraining the variances to be non-negative and refitting the linear growth model.  I think that it is fair to say that majority opinion has come down on the side that this is not good general practice because it tends to hide problems with the model.  However, in your situation, it may be a useful follow-up to fitting the model without the non-negativitiy constraints.  It might not converge at all but it if does it may give you a poorly fitting solution that passes basic admissibility tests.

I am not a statistician but it seems to me that the following logic holds.  The inadmissible solution represents the best obtainable fit (assuming you get a consistent solution) for the unconstrained linear growth model.  As such, any admissible solution would have to fit worse.  So, if the nonlinear growth model fits better at a statistically significant level, then it must also fit better than any admissible solution for the linear growth model.  However, it may be helpful to compare the inadmissible solution to an admissible solution with constraints, because you would not accept the inadmissible solution even if it fit well, or within sampling error of the non-linear growth model.  Perhaps others can comment on the behavior of chi-square for inadmissible solutions and the validity of such chi-square difference tests.

Keith
